extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate students in probability and stochastic processes
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter material giving precise conditions and results for renewal theory (renewal measure, renewal equation, Blackwell's and renewal theorems), large deviation rates for sums of i.i.d. random variables (Cramér-type results), and the De Moivre–Laplace central limit approximation together with the notion of weak convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renewal measure U definition
rubrics_metrics.description: U(A) = sum_{n=0}^∞ P(T_n ∈ A). In particular U(t) is shorthand for U([0,t]) and equals E N_t (the expected number of renewals up to t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat U as a measure (distribution function U(t)=U([0,t])). Use this to express convolutions and renewal equations; e.g., U = 1_{[0,∞)} + U * F (equation (2.6.2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymptotic renewal rate (Theorem 2.6.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: As t → ∞, U(t)/t → 1/μ (where μ = E ξ_i is the mean interarrival time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Wald's equation applied to the stopping time N_t and truncation/approximation arguments (ξ ∧ c) to handle unbounded ξ. Holds in the general cases treated (arguments handle μ finite; inequalities trivial when μ = ∞). Useful lower and upper bounds: t/E(ξ_i ∧ t) ≤ U(t) ≤ 2t/E(ξ_i ∧ t) (Exercise 2.6.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonarithmetic vs arithmetic distribution condition
rubrics_metrics.description: The asymptotic behavior of the renewal measure depends on whether F is arithmetic (concentrated on {δ,2δ,...}) or nonarithmetic (not arithmetic). Many limit results (e.g., Blackwell's renewal theorem and the renewal theorem) are stated for the nonarithmetic case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When F is arithmetic treat separately (often via discrete methods/Markov chains). For the continuous/nonarithmetic case theorems give limits of U([t,t+h]) and convolutional limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blackwell's renewal theorem (Theorem 2.6.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F is nonarithmetic then U([t, t + h]) → h/μ as t → ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two proofs presented depending on μ finite or infinite: for μ<∞ via coupling with a stationary renewal process (delay distribution G defined below); for μ=∞ an argument adapted from Feller using lim sup/lim inf and support properties. The coupling construction and bounds (involving a coupling time J,K and bounding P(T_J>t)→0) are used to compare stationary and ordinary processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stationary renewal process / delay distribution G (equation (2.6.4))
rubrics_metrics.description: The delay distribution G that yields a stationary renewal process is G(t) = (1/μ) ∫_0^t (1 − F(y)) dy (this defines a probability distribution because μ = ∫_0^∞ (1 − F(y)) dy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the interarrival distribution is exponential (Poisson process) this G equals F. Use G to construct delayed (stationary) renewal processes and to obtain V(t)=E N_t for delayed processes via convolution V = G * U.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renewal equation H = h + H * F and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: The renewal equation is H = h + H * F, e.g., U(t) = 1 + ∫_0^t U(t − s) dF(s) (h ≡ 1), and V(t) = G(t) + ∫_0^t V(t − s) dF(s) (h = G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many problems reduce to casting a quantity as the solution of a renewal equation; then apply existence/uniqueness and asymptotic theorems (Theorem 2.6.9 and Theorem 2.6.12). Examples include pedestrian delay, ruin probabilities (Cramér's transform leading to a renewal equation), and alternating renewal processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and uniqueness for bounded h (Theorem 2.6.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If h is bounded then H(t) = ∫_0^t h(t − s) dU(s) is the unique solution of the renewal equation H = h + H * F that is bounded on bounded intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct H_n via finite sums H_n = sum_{m=0}^n (h * F^{m*}) and let n→∞. Uniqueness follows because a bounded-on-bounded-intervals solution K satisfying K = K * F iterated gives K * F^{n*} → 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Riemann integrability and criterion (definition + Lemma 2.6.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: A function h on [0,∞) is directly Riemann integrable (d.R.i.) if upper and lower Riemann sums I^δ and I_δ (sums of sup/inf over intervals [kδ,(k+1)δ)) both approach the same finite limit as δ → 0. If h ≥ 0 is decreasing with h(0) < ∞ and ∫_0^∞ h(x) dx < ∞, then h is directly Riemann integrable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notion is 'direct' because the integral over [0,∞) is approximated directly by Riemann sums on the infinite interval rather than via limiting integrals on finite intervals. This hypothesis is used in the renewal theorem to guarantee the required integrability and uniform approximation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renewal theorem (Theorem 2.6.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F is nonarithmetic and h is directly Riemann integrable then H(t) = ∫_0^t h(t − s) dU(s) → (1/μ) ∫_0^∞ h(s) ds as t → ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuition: by Theorem 2.6.9 H is the convolution of h with U and by Blackwell (dU(s) → ds/μ) the integral tends to (1/μ)∫ h. Proof handles simple step functions first and then approximates general h by Riemann sums; Lemma 2.6.13 provides a useful sufficient condition for d.R.i.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residual/age/forward recurrence distributions (applications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Example results: For h(t)=1 − F(t + x), P(T_{N(t)} − t > x) → (1/μ) ∫_x^∞ (1 − F(t)) dt as t→∞ (residual waiting time converges to the delay distribution). Similarly age A_t = t − T_{N(t)-1} has limiting distribution P(A_t > x) → (1/μ) ∫_x^∞ (1 − F(t)) dt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are standard applications of the renewal theorem and the renewal equation. They show convergence of local functionals (age, excess) to explicit limits under the nonarithmetic + μ<∞ assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subadditivity lemma for large deviations (Lemma 2.7.1) / definition of γ(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define γ_n = log π_n with π_n = P(S_n ≥ n a). If γ_{m+n} ≥ γ_m + γ_n then γ_n/n → sup_m γ_m/m. Hence γ(a) := lim_{n→∞} (1/n) log P(S_n ≥ n a) exists (≤ 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is based on multiplicativity π_{m+n} ≥ π_m π_n (independence) and transforms to subadditivity of logs. It provides existence of exponential rates for tail probabilities irrespective of finiteness of mgf.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chernoff/Cramér upper bound via mgf (inequality (2.7.2))
rubrics_metrics.description: If φ(θ) = E e^{θ X_i} < ∞ for some θ > 0, then for any θ>0: P(S_n ≥ n a) ≤ exp(−n{a θ − κ(θ)}), where κ(θ)=log φ(θ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is obtained by Markov's inequality applied to e^{θ S_n}. Optimizing over θ gives the best exponential (Chernoff) upper bound and leads to identification of the rate function when the optimizing θ exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moment-generating-function condition (H1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothesis (H1): φ(θ) = E e^{θ X_i} < ∞ for some θ > 0. This implies tails decay exponentially and EX^+ < ∞, so μ = E X exists in [−∞,∞].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: H1 is the standard Cramér condition that ensures large deviation exponential rates (allowing application of mgf-based Chernoff bounds and change-of-measure tilting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nondegeneracy condition (H2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothesis (H2): F is not a point mass at μ. Under H2, κ'(θ) = φ'(θ)/φ(θ) is strictly increasing (variance under the tilted measure > 0) and aθ − κ(θ) is strictly concave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: H2 ensures uniqueness of the solution θ_a to κ'(θ)=a when it exists, which in turn identifies the unique optimizing tilt for the large deviation rate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tilted distribution F_θ and relation to κ'(θ)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define F_θ(x) via dF_θ(x) = e^{θ x} dF(x) / φ(θ). Its mean is κ'(θ) = φ'(θ)/φ(θ), and its variance = φ''(θ)/φ(θ) − (φ'(θ)/φ(θ))^2 ≥ 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tilted measure is used in the change-of-measure proof of the matching lower bound for large deviations (Theorem 2.7.7). Monotonicity of κ'(θ) follows from positivity of this variance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cramér's theorem in the solvable case (Theorem 2.7.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (H1) and (H2) hold and there exists θ_a ∈ (0, θ^+) solving κ'(θ_a) = a, then γ(a) = lim_{n→∞} (1/n) log P(S_n ≥ n a) = −a θ_a + κ(θ_a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Upper bound from Chernoff. Lower bound via change-of-measure to F_λ (λ>θ_a) and weak law under the tilted measure. Examples computed: normal (θ_a=a gives γ(a)=−a^2/2), exponential, coin flips (explicit formulas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior when support is bounded (Theorem 2.7.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If x_0 = sup{x : F(x) < 1} < ∞ and F is not concentrated at x_0 then φ(θ) < ∞ for all θ>0 and κ'(θ)/→ x_0 as θ→∞. For a = x_0 the trivial rate γ(a) = log P(X_i = x_0) applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This covers the case when the underlying variable is bounded above: the tilting mean approaches the supremum of support as θ→∞; limits at the boundary can be deduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear regime when mgf radius finite (Theorem 2.7.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If x_0 = ∞, θ^+ < ∞ and κ'(θ) increases to a finite limit a_0 as θ ↑ θ^+, then for any a ≥ a_0, γ(a) = −a θ^+ + κ(θ^+) (i.e., γ is linear for a ≥ a_0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This handles the case where the mgf is finite only up to θ^+ and the tilt cannot achieve means beyond a_0; the large-deviation rate becomes linear beyond that threshold. Proof again uses change-of-measure with θ↑θ^+ and local estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: De Moivre–Laplace central limit approximation (Theorem 3.1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For i.i.d. Rademacher variables X_i (P=1/2 ±1) and S_n = sum X_i, as n→∞ P(a ≤ S_n/√n ≤ b) → ∫_a^b (2π)^{-1/2} e^{-x^2/2} dx.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from Stirling's formula approximating binomial coefficients; general central limit theorems in later sections extend this to wider classes of i.i.d. variables. The local limit P(S_{2n}=2k) ∼ (π n)^{-1/2} e^{-x^2/2} when 2k/√(2n)→x is shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and basic properties of weak convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence of distribution functions F_n converges weakly to F (F_n ⇒ F) if F_n(y) → F(y) for all y that are continuity points of F. Random variables X_n converge in distribution if their distribution functions converge weakly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convergence is only required at continuity points of the limit. Examples illustrate necessity (e.g., X + 1/n gives F_n(x)=F(x−1/n) which converges only at continuity points). Weak convergence is the topology used for CLT statements.
